passage1.text: Having a rival can keep you committed to achieving your goals and enhance your overall performance. But before you go out and find an entrepreneur to outcompete, it's important to understand and avoid the traps that often come with rivalry. After all, competitive rivalry can also hinder effective decision-making and increase your willingness to take risks, behaviors that can ultimately hurt your venture's success. Finding someone you're committed to outcompeting can be a great way to stay focused on your goals and push your venture to the next level. But when you're intently focused on outperforming your rivals, you may begin to develop a "win-at-all-costs" mentality that causes you to ignore how you achieve success. One group of researchers, for example, examined the link between rivalry and unethical behavior. They found that when people compete against their rivals, they are more willing to behave unethically to win. But such behavior may stain your reputation and strain relationships important to your success. One way to avoid this trap is to stop and reflect on what's important. While outperforming your rivals may provide short-term benefits, the loss of your integrity will have long-term consequences. One reason having a rival can enhance your venture's performance is that it creates a level of excitement that drives you to work harder. But this eagerness to win may also hurt your venture's success, particularly when it causes you to make impulsive, insensible decisions. But it's possible to avoid such costly mistakes by making a habit of engaging in critical thinking, such as considering opposing viewpoints and conducting cost-benefit analyses, especially for those decisions that are complex and can determine the future of your venture. The sense of eagerness that comes with having a rival can not only cause you to make poorer decisions, but it can also lead you to take greater risks that put your venture in peril. One way you can overcome the risk-inducing effects of rivalry that stand to endanger your venture's success is to remain attentive to your emotional state and actively monitor how such feelings are affecting your decision-making.

passage2.text: A multitasker is one who can perform two or more tasks effectively at the same time, which—apart from the obvious differences—is similar to what a computer does. The concept does indeed come from the realms of technology, where it is used to refer to an operating system that can execute multiple tasks at the same time. However, the question is: can a person really be a multitasker? For most scientists, the answer is no. So much so that, according to experts in neuroscience (神经系统科学), our brains do not handle multitasking situations well. As soon as two tasks require our attention, productivity suffers. What we call multitasking, therefore, is in reality the ability to move more or less quickly from one task to another. This requires two essential conditions: that one of the tasks needs to be automatic, like walking or eating, and that they both need different mental processes. Answering the phone and writing at the same time, for example. However, on the other side of the coin there are people who maintain that it is possible to be, or at least seem to be, multitasking. A recent study concluded that regardless of whether people are actually handling several tasks or not, the mere fact that they perceive this activity as multitasking has a positive effect on their performance. The business perspective offers a different view: multitasking is understood as the ability to adapt to all types of environment within a company and effectively undertake different activities within a set time frame. Indeed, many companies look for people who are skilled in multitasking to improve their productivity. From this different perspective, you can not only be multitasking but this ability can also be taught: something that is easier in fluid organisations, which favour flexibility in their working practices. The benefits of multitasking are clear. Being quicker and more efficient increases our performance and the number of tasks completed. But having to pay attention to several things at once means that the powers of concentration are reduced and that can lead to more mistakes.

paragraphs.A: Attitudes towards paternity leave (陪产假) have drastically changed in America in the last five years as more fathers feel comfortable taking extended time off, but gender bias persists when it comes to career prospects and the home, according to a new study of working parents.
paragraphs.B: Research by the Boston College Center for Work & Family, which surveyed new parents at four large US companies who were qualified for taking at least six weeks paid parental leave, found that 81% of the 1,240employees surveyed said the notion of fathers taking leave has become more acceptable.
paragraphs.C: Of those surveyed, 62% of fathers took the maximum amount of time off compared to 93% of mothers, and around three-quarters of workers said their employer was equally supportive of mothers and fathers taking parental leave and over half said leave policies had made workplace culture better.
paragraphs.D: The US is one of only three countries in the world not to offer statutory (法定的) paid leave, but increasingly states and companies are starting to take up the issue. So far, eight states and the District of Columbia have their own paid family leave laws.
paragraphs.E: Brad Harrington, executive director of the center and lead author of the study, estimates only 20% to 30%of companies in the US offer paid parental leave. He feels the research findings reflect an obvious change in corporate attitudes to new fathers taking time off.
paragraphs.F: "We did a study on paternity leave five years ago. Compared with those findings, these numbers were shocking to me. I did not expect 80% of people to say the organisation finds dads taking this leave acceptable and three-quarters to say it's equally supportive of women and men taking leave," Harrington said.
paragraphs.G: The previous study found that nearly three-quarters of fathers saw two to four weeks as an appropriate duration for paternity leave and 76% said they would prefer not to take all their time off at once.
paragraphs.H: Since then, there have been a number of legal cases against companies involving paternity leave—including cases against JPMorgan Chase and Estée Lauder—which have helped put pressure on companies to make their parental leave policies gender neutral.
paragraphs.I: However, the study also shows how traditional gender roles endure both at work, where more women than men reported changes in their perceived career potential, and at home—even among workers who claim to have a strong desire for equality.
paragraphs.J: The vast majority of men, 97%, said one of the top reasons to take leave was to share caregiving with their partner. But when they were asked about how caregiving and household tasks were divided, their answers painted a different picture. While about 75% of employees said both genders should give the same amount of care, the majority of men and nearly half of women admitted that in reality the female actually did most of it. A tiny fraction, 2%, of men said they did more of the childcare.
paragraphs.K: Men and women's experiences of the return to work following parental leave were also considerably different. Of the women surveyed, 32% reported a downturn in their job satisfaction, while 14% said it increased. In comparison, 17% of men said their job satisfaction went down and 20% said it went up. Meanwhile, more women reported an increase in their responsibilities and manager expectations after childbirth. Half of the women said they used flexible work arrangements after becoming a parent, while just 27% of men did. Similar percentages of men and women said they enjoyed their careers and that it gave them a sense of achievement, while around half of women and 44% of men said it was a key part of their identity.
paragraphs.L: On the subject of career advancement, 59% of women and 49% of men said leave could be limiting and both genders said they feared it would have an impact on their progress long-term. But on opportunity for promotion, more than double the number of women, 30% compared with 15% of men, believed their chances to be lower after becoming a parent. Despite progress, the struggle for women to reach the highest positions of power is demonstrated in this year's Fortune 500 list, which featured a record 33 female CEOs, but this still represents a tiny fraction of the total. M) Harrington said culture change depends on companies putting more focus on men and their responsibilities. "By that I mean companies need to give men paternity leave and encourage men to take time off to be with their kids early on in the kids' life. They also need to recognise that men have to make significant adjustments when they become parents. Companies cannot do all these things to enhance women's advancement and then turn around and say, ‘Oh, but we don't expect the men to take over for the women at home." N) In May, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and Outten & Golden LLP announced a historic class-action $5m settlement with JPMorgan Chase on behalf of male employees who claim they were illegally denied access to paid parental leave. Derek Rotondo, 35, filed the discrimination charge against his company after he was allegedly told by his HR department that mothers were considered primary caregivers. Thus, they were allowed to take 16 weeks of paid parental leave. Fathers, however, could take just two weeks. O) The father of two from Columbus, Ohio, who still works at the company as an associate and investigator, said he has witnessed a “domino effect (多米诺效应)” across companies since the settlement, but that there is still substantial progress to be made towards changing attitudes towards paternity leave. P) "I do think there's still some way to go...there's still going to be sort of the unstated expectation for new dads to essentially come right back to work, but I think the research is showing that's starting to change." He said equal parental leave is an essential component to creating gender equality in the workplace. "The old standard of women staying home, having babies and cooking doesn't apply and hasn't applied for a long time."

questions.script:
Mobile phones have changed the way we live, how we read, work, communicate, and shop. But we already
know this. [3] What we have not yet understood is the way the tiny machines in front of us are changing our skeletons,
possibly altering not just the way we behave but even the very shape of our bodies.
New scientific research at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Queensland, Australia, suggests that young people
are developing extra pieces of bone at the backs of their heads. These pieces of bone are caused by the way people bend their
heads when they use the phone. This shifts weight onto the muscles at the back of the head and causes the bone to grow in
a way that is not normal. [4] This process can be compared to the way the skin hardens in response to constant rubbing or
pressure. The result is a piece of bone like a horn that sticks out from the head by the neck.

questions.script:
[16] Artificial intelligence agents play ever more influential roles in our lives. They do everything from suggesting
new friends to recommending purchases. They're even beginning to drive our cars. Another role that they are expected
to take over is negotiating on our behalf in commercial transactions or legal disputes. [17] So, it's important to know
whether using an artificial intelligence agent might affect how we negotiate. Research indicates that it does. In a new
study, participants were told to imagine that they were negotiating for something important to them, like a house. Next,
they were told either that they would negotiate for themselves, or they would program an artificial intelligence agent
to negotiate for them. Participants then completed a survey indicating how tough, deceptive and pleasant or otherwise
they wanted to be, or wanted their agent to be, in the negotiations. For example, participants could choose to be tough
by making an opening demand far greater than what they'd be willing to accept. They could also choose to express
sympathy with their opponent to appear pleasant. But they could also indicate that they or their agent—would strategically express anger toward the opponent to gain advantage, or they could opt to convey dissatisfaction with the encounter so that the other party would think they were losing interest. These are both examples of deceptive strategies. [18] Participants were more willing to employ deceptive strategies when assigned an agent to negotiate on their behalf.

questions.script:
New research has studied the effects of a seven-week healthy cooking course. Academics measured the program's
effect on cooking confidence and self-perceived mental health. Researchers also measured participants'overall
satisfaction around cooking and diet-related behaviors.
What were the findings? Course participants saw significant improvements in general health. They also reported
improved mental health and subjective vitality immediately after the program. [19] These benefits remained six months
after the completion of the course.
What caused these improvements? Researchers have previously found a link between eating more fruits and vegetables, and improved longer term mental health. This would imply that the participants in the current study may have felt better due to improved diet.
However, the study showed participants'mental health improved even if their reported diet did not change after
completing the program. Also, the mental health benefits were equal among participants who were overweight or obese,
and those in a healthy weight range. [20] This suggests a link between cooking confidence and satisfaction around
cooking, and mental health benefits.
[21] Who benefits most from learning to cook? Gender plays a part. At the start of the program, 77 per cent of
female participants were confident about cooking, but just 23 per cent of males were confident. At the end of the
program, cooking confidence and skills were equal across both counterparts. This change in confidence could lead to a
gender balance in home cooking.This in turn could reduce consumption of unhealthy,high-calorie processed meals.

questions.script:
[22] What is personal space? We often think of it as an invisible bubble of space surrounding us that others can't
enter, without causing discomfort. Research shows, however, that we actually have bubbles of different sizes. Each of
these bubbles applies to a different set of people.
The smallest zone, called "intimate space", extends outward from our bodies 18 inches in every direction
Only family, pets and one's closest friends may enter it. [23]A mere acquaintance entering our intimate space makes
us uncomfortable. Next is the bubble called personal space", extending from 1.5 feet to 4 feet away. Friends and
acquaintances can comfortably occupy this zone, especially during informal conversations, but strangers are forbidden.
[24] Extending from 4 to 12 feet away from us is “"social space". Here people feel comfortable conducting routine
social interactions with new acquaintances or total strangers.
Those are the average sizes of American's personal bubbles, anyway. It is important to keep in mind that personal
space varies depending on culture and context. Furthermore, there are significant individual differences. As we all
know, cultural or individual differences in personal bubble diameters are all too often the cause of discomfort. How did
these personal bubbles arise? According to research, we begin to develop our individual sense of personal space around
age 3 or 4. [25] The sizes of our bubbles are fixed by our teens. These bubbles are constructed and monitored by the
brain region involved in fear.

[22] What is personal space? We often think of it as an invisible bubble of space surrounding us that others can't
enter, without causing discomfort. Research shows, however, that we actually have bubbles of different sizes. Each of
these bubbles applies to a different set of people.
The smallest zone, called "intimate space", extends outward from our bodies 18 inches in every direction
Only family, pets and one's closest friends may enter it. [23]A mere acquaintance entering our intimate space makes
us uncomfortable. Next is the bubble called personal space", extending from 1.5 feet to 4 feet away. Friends and
acquaintances can comfortably occupy this zone, especially during informal conversations, but strangers are forbidden.
[24] Extending from 4 to 12 feet away from us is “"social space". Here people feel comfortable conducting routine
social interactions with new acquaintances or total strangers.
Those are the average sizes of American's personal bubbles, anyway. It is important to keep in mind that personal
space varies depending on culture and context. Furthermore, there are significant individual differences. As we all
know, cultural or individual differences in personal bubble diameters are all too often the cause of discomfort. How did
these personal bubbles arise? According to research, we begin to develop our individual sense of personal space around
age 3 or 4. [25] The sizes of our bubbles are fixed by our teens. These bubbles are constructed and monitored by the
brain region involved in fear.
questions.expl: 短文明确说明“4到12英尺的距离是‘社交空间’，在这里，人们与新认识的人或陌生人进行日常社交会感到舒适”，B项正确。A项“个人空间”适用于朋友和熟人；C项“18英寸内”是亲密空间；D项“超过2英尺”范围模糊（社交空间是4-12英尺），排除。 涉及知识点：听力短文空间分类与适用场景的对应，精准匹配不同空间的距离与功能。

questions.stem: 第 26 空
questions.expl: 详解：语法判断：空格所在句子结构完整，需填副词。语义判断：首句提到“许多研究关注家庭生活对工作的影响”，空格句以“然而”转折，意为“关于休闲活动影响的研究却很少”，前后语义对比强烈，“surprisingly”（令人惊讶地）符合语境，体现“研究数量少”的意外性。 涉及知识点：副词的语法功能（修饰整个句子）、转折关系的语义衔接。

questions.stem: 第 27 空
questions.expl: (shaped) 详解：语法判断：空格所在宾语从句缺少谓语，主语是“the time”，句子时态为一般过去时，需填动词过去式。语义判断：句子意为“研究他们花在业余爱好上的时间如何影响工作生活”，“shaped”（影响；塑造）符合“时间对工作生活产生作用”的语境。 涉及知识点：动词的时态一致、谓语动词的语义搭配（time + shape + work life）。

questions.stem: 第 28 空
questions.expl: (normal) 详解：语法判断：空格前为介词“than”，后接“on their leisure activity”，需填名词。语义判断：句子意为“当参与者在休闲活动上花的时间比平常多时，工作能力信心增强”，“normal”（常态）构成“longer than normal”（比正常时间更长）的固定搭配，符合语境。 涉及知识点：名词的语义辨析、固定短语搭配（longer than normal）。

questions.stem: 第 29 空
questions.expl: (case) 详解：语法判断：空格前为定冠词“the”，后接“when”引导的状语从句，需填名词。语义判断：句子意为“但只有在两种情况下才会出现这种（信心增强的）情况”，“case”（情况；状况）符合“指代前文提到的积极结果”的语境。 涉及知识点：名词的语义指代功能、“the case when...”的句型搭配。

questions.stem: 第 30 空
questions.expl: (casually) 详解：语法判断：空格所在句子结构完整，需填副词。语义判断：前文提到“认真对待的爱好”，此处通过“but”转折，意为“爱好与工作相似但只是随便做做”，“casually”（随便地）与“serious”（认真的）形成对比，符合逻辑。 涉及知识点：副词的语义辨析、转折关系的语义对比。

questions.stem: 第 31 空
questions.expl: 详解：语法判断：空格前为“their work”，需填名词。语义判断：句子意为“如果爱好既认真又与工作相似，花更多时间会降低工作效率”，“efficiency”（效率）构成“work efficiency”（工作效率）的固定搭配，符合“精力分散影响工作效果”的语境。 涉及知识点：名词的语义搭配（work + efficiency）、上下文逻辑推导（精力投入冲突→效率下降）。

questions.stem: 第 32 空
questions.expl: (exhausted) 详解：语法判断：空格前为“they may be left”，后接“and unable to...”，“leave sb. + 形容词”表示“使某人处于某种状态”，需填形容词或分词。语义判断：句子意为“如果爱好与工作有同样要求，人们可能会筋疲力尽，无法做好工作”，“exhausted”（筋疲力尽的）符合“心理资源过度消耗”的语境。 涉及知识点：“leave + 宾语 + 宾语补足语”的语法结构、形容词的语义搭配（描述人的状态）。

questions.expl: (interfere) 详解：语法判断：空格前为“it may not”，后接“in the same way”，需填动词原形。语义判断：句子通过“but instead”转折，意为“如果爱好与工作完全不同，可能不会以同样方式干扰工作，反而帮助拓展技能”，“interfere”（干扰）与后文“help”形成对比，符合逻辑。 涉及知识点：动词的语法功能（情态动词后接原形）、转折关系的语义对比（interfere vs. help）。

questions.expl: (boost) 详解：语法判断：空格前为“that can”，后接“their confidence”，需填动词原形。语义判断：句子意为“爱好拓展其他知识技能，从而增强工作信心”，“boost”（增强；促进）符合“技能提升→信心增强”的逻辑，与前文“strengthened their belief”形成呼应。 涉及知识点：动词的语义搭配（boost + confidence）、因果关系的语义衔接（develop skills → boost confidence）。

questions.expl: (removed) 详解：语法判断：空格前为“is so far”，后接“from their day-to-day work activities”，需填形容词或分词。语义判断：句子意为“攀岩与日常工作活动迥然不同”，“be far removed from”（与……迥然不同）为固定短语，符合“爱好与工作无重叠”的语境，解释了“仍有精力恢复工作”的原因。 涉及知识点：固定短语搭配（be far removed from）、形容词性分词的语义功能。

questions.stem: 36. In the absence of Federal legislation, some states in the US have passed laws concerning paid family leave.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“无联邦立法”“美国一些州通过带薪家庭休假法律”。定位到D段：“美国是仅有的三个不提供法定带薪休假的国家之一，但越来越多的州开始关注该问题，八个州和哥伦比亚特区有自己的带薪家庭休假法”。题干是对该段的同义转述，其中“Inthe absence of Federal legislation”对应“not to offer statutory paid leave”，“some states”对应“eight states and the District of Columbia”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的同义转述识别，关注“联邦与州”的立法差异。

questions.stem: 37. Most fathers admitted that even during their paternity leave they actually did much less childcare than the mother.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“大多数父亲承认”“陪产假期间照顾孩子比母亲少”。定位到J段：“75%的员工表示男女应给予同等看护，但大多数男性和近一半女性承认，现实中女性做了大部分看护工作”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“Most fathers”对应“the majority of men”，“did much less childcare than the mother”对应“the female actually did most of it”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的语义概括，区分“理想认知”与“现实情况”。

questions.stem: 38. According to one father, equal parental leave is indispensable to achieving gender equality in the workplace.
questions.expl: 题干译文根据一位父亲的说法，平等的育儿假对于实现职场中的性别平等是必不可少的。 答案解析P。由题千关键信息onefather、parental leave、anessential component和achievinggenderequalityin theworkplace定位到P段。该段进一步论述了D段中那位父亲的观点，第二句提到：他说，平等的育儿假是 创造职场性别平等的必要组成部分。由此可知，题干是对该句内容的同义转述。题干中的onefather对应 原文中的He（即前文中提到的DerekRotondo），而equalparentalleaveisindispensabletoachievinggender equality in the workplace对应原文中的equal parental leave is an essential component to creating gender equality in theworkplaceo 四级2023.12第二营31

questions.stem: 39. One survey indicated there is now less objection to paternity leave.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“一项调查”“反对陪产假的人变少”。定位到B段：“波士顿学院的调查发现，81%的受访者表示父亲休陪产假的观念变得更容易接受了”，即“反对者变少”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“One survey indicated”对应“Research...found”，“less objection”对应“more acceptable”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的语义转换，将“接受度提高”转化为“反对者减少”。

questions.stem: 40. Compared to five years ago, according to one researcher, many more people said their organisation gave the same support to men and women taking parental leave.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“五年前”“研究人员”“公司对男女育儿假支持相同”。定位到F段：哈林顿提到“五年前做过相关研究，如今80%的人认为公司接受父亲休产假，四分之三的人认为公司对男女支持相同”。题干是对该句的概括，“Compared to five years ago”对应“Compared with those findings”，“one researcher”对应“Harrington”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的时间对比与观点概括，关注研究结果的变化趋势。

questions.stem: 41. One study finds that even workers who claim to desire gender equality stick to traditional gender roles both at work and at home.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“一项研究”“渴望性别平等的员工”“坚持传统性别角色”。定位到I段：“研究显示，传统性别角色在工作和家庭中持续存在，即使是声称强烈渴望平等的员工也是如此”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“One study finds”对应“the study also shows”，“stick to traditional gender roles”对应“endure”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的细节精准定位，捕捉“even”引导的递进关系。

questions.stem: 42. The majority of workers surveyed said parental leave policies had improved workplace culture.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“大多数受访者”“育儿假政策改善职场文化”。定位到C段：“超过一半的受访者表示，休育儿假的政策使得职场文化得到了改善”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“The majority of workers surveyed”对应“Of those surveyed...over half”，“improved workplace culture”对应“made workplace culture better”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的数量表述转换，“over half”与“the majority”的语义对应。

questions.stem: 43. In spite of progress, the number of women in top positions of big companies remains extremely small.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“尽管有进步”“大公司高层女性数量少”。定位到L段：“尽管取得了进步，但《财富》500强中女性CEO仅33位，占比极小”。题干是对该句的概括，“In spite of progress”对应“Despite progress”，“top positions of big companies”对应“the highest positions of power”，“remains extremely small”对应“a tiny fraction”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的语义概括，将具体案例（财富500强女性CEO）转化为普遍结论。

questions.stem: 44. According to one estimate, less than one third of companies in the US provide paid parental leave.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“一项估计”“美国不到三分之一公司提供带薪育儿假”。定位到E段：“哈林顿估计，美国只有20%到30%的公司提供带薪育儿假”，20%-30%即“不到三分之一”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“one estimate”对应“estimates”，“less than one third”对应“20% to 30%”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的数字转换与语义对应，将百分比转化为分数表述。

questions.stem: 45. A number of lawsuits have pressured companies to formulate gender neutral policies on parental leave.
questions.expl: 题干关键信息：“一些诉讼”“迫使公司制定性别中立育儿假政策”。定位到H段：“多起涉及陪产假的法律案件（如摩根大通、雅诗兰黛案），帮助施压公司制定性别中立的育儿假政策”。题干是对该句的同义转述，“Anumber of lawsuits”对应“a number of legal cases”，“formulate gender neutral policies”对应“make their parental leave policies gender neutral”。 涉及知识点：信息匹配题的因果关系定位，关注“legal cases”与“policy changes”的关联。

questions.stem: 46. How can competitive rivalry benefit entrepreneurs according to the passage?

options.A: By enabling them to outcompete other entrepreneurs.
options.B: By enabling them to make their venture a success.
options.C: By helping them to reach long-term goals.
options.D: By helping them to stay goal-oriented.

questions.expl: 定位到第一段第一句：“拥有一个竞争对手可以让你致力于实现自己的目标并提升整体表现”，核心益处是“帮助保持以目标为导向”，D项正确。A项“超越其他企业家”是竞争的行为而非益处；B项“使企业成功”与原文“竞争可能最终损害企业成功”相悖；C项“实现长期目标”未提及（原文强调“专注目标”而非“实现长期目标”），排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，定位原文核心观点句，排除语义扩大或相悖的选项。

questions.stem: 47. What is one of the traps entrepreneurs may often fall into when competing with rivals?

options.A: They may adopt strategies that are bound to ruin their venture.
options.B: They may resort to unethical means to outperform their rivals.
options.C: They may be too eager to succeed while ignoring the huge labor cost.
options.D: They may be intently focused on winning at the current market level.

questions.expl: 定位到第二段第四句：“当与竞争对手竞争时，人们更愿意为了赢得胜利而做出不道德的行为”，这是竞争中常见的陷阱，B项正确。A项“必然毁掉企业”过于绝对（原文仅说“玷污声誉、紧张关系”）；C项“忽略人力成本”、D项“专注当前市场水平获胜”未提及，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，定位“trap”对应的具体内容，关注“for example”引导的例证支撑。

questions.stem: 48. What are entrepreneurs advised to do to avoid traps that often accompany rivalry?

options.A: Deliberate on what really matters.
options.B: Prioritize reaping immediate benefits.
options.C: Estimate the long-term consequences.
options.D: Reflect on what successes are achievable.

questions.expl: 定位到第二段倒数第二句：“避免掉进这个陷阱的一个方法是停下来，反思一下什么才是重要的”，A项“慎重考虑什么才是真正重要的事”与原文“reflect on what's important”同义，正确。B项“优先获取眼前利益”与原文“短期利益不如正直重要”相悖；C项“估计长期后果”是反思后的结果而非方法；D项“反思可实现的成功”未提及，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，定位“one way to avoid”引导的解决方案，注意同义替换（deliberate on = reflect on）。

questions.stem: 49. How can entrepreneurs avoid making impulsive and insensible decisions?

options.A: By engaging themselves in critical reasoning.
options.B: By developing a habit of keeping their integrity.
options.C: By criticizing themselves for previous poor performances.
options.D: By refraining from being too excited about their successes.

questions.expl: 定位到第三段第三句：“通过养成进行批判性思考的习惯，可以避免冲动、不明智的决策”，A项“进行批判性论证”与“critical thinking”同义，正确。B项“保持正直的习惯”是避免不道德行为的方法；C项“批评以前的糟糕表现”、D项“不过度兴奋于成功”未提及，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，区分不同陷阱的对应解决方案，关注“such as”引导的例证解释。

questions.stem: 50. How can entrepreneurs overcome the risk-inducing effects of rivalry?

options.A: By paying close attention to their current performance.
options.B: By taking steps that stand to endanger their rivals' success.
options.C: By monitoring how their decision-making impacts their mentality.
options.D: By keeping their emotions in check to avoid making poor decisions.

questions.expl: 定位到最后一段最后一句：“克服竞争的风险诱发效应的方法是密切关注情绪状态，并监控情绪如何影响决策”，即“约束情绪以避免错误决策”，D项正确。A项“关注当前表现”与原文“关注情绪”不符；B项“危及对手成功”未提及且不道德；C项“监控决策影响心态”与原文“监控情绪影响决策”逻辑颠倒，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，定位“one way to overcome”引导的解决方案，注意逻辑关系的正向匹配。

questions.stem: 51. What does a “multitasker” originally refer to?

options.A: An operating system capable of doing several tasks at once.
options.B: A skilled worker executing more than one task at the same time.
options.C: A sophisticated technology doing several tasks effectively at once.
options.D: An efficient person able to perform multiple tasks at the same time.

questions.expl: 定位到第一段第二句：“多重任务处理的概念源自技术领域，用来指代可以同时执行多项任务的操作系统”，明确说明最初所指，A项正确。B项“技术工人”、C项“复杂技术”未提及；D项“高效人士”是该概念后来用于人的含义，而非“最初所指”，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，关注“originally refer to”对应的“come from”“used to refer to”等关键词，区分概念的原始含义与延伸含义。

questions.stem: 52. Why can't people really be multitaskers according to neuroscientists?

options.A: They are not sufficiently exposed to multitasking situations.
options.B: They are not comparable to mechanical operating systems.
options.C: Their brains do not allow them to multitask.
options.D: Their attention span cannot be expanded.

questions.expl: 定位到第二段第二句：“根据神经系统科学专家的说法，我们的大脑无法很好地处理多重任务的情况”，直接说明原因是“大脑不允许”，C项正确。A项“接触不足”、B项“无法与操作系统相比”、D项“注意力范围无法扩大”均未提及，排除。 涉及知识点：阅读理解细节题，定位“neuroscientists”对应的专家观点句，提取核心原因。

questions.stem: 53. What do we learn from the conclusion of a recent study on multitasking?

options.A: People make greater achievements by maintaining whatever they are doing is multitasking.
options.B: People's performance benefits from the perception of what they are doing as multitasking.

[16] Artificial intelligence agents play ever more influential roles in our lives. They do everything from suggesting
new friends to recommending purchases. They're even beginning to drive our cars. Another role that they are expected
to take over is negotiating on our behalf in commercial transactions or legal disputes. [17] So, it's important to know
whether using an artificial intelligence agent might affect how we negotiate. Research indicates that it does. In a new
study, participants were told to imagine that they were negotiating for something important to them, like a house. Next,
they were told either that they would negotiate for themselves, or they would program an artificial intelligence agent
to negotiate for them. Participants then completed a survey indicating how tough, deceptive and pleasant or otherwise
they wanted to be, or wanted their agent to be, in the negotiations. For example, participants could choose to be tough
by making an opening demand far greater than what they'd be willing to accept. They could also choose to express
sympathy with their opponent to appear pleasant. But they could also indicate that they or their agent—would strategically express anger toward the opponent to gain advantage, or they could opt to convey dissatisfaction with the encounter so that the other party would think they were losing interest. These are both examples of deceptive strategies. [18] Participants were more willing to employ deceptive strategies when assigned an agent to negotiate on their behalf.

New research has studied the effects of a seven-week healthy cooking course. Academics measured the program's
effect on cooking confidence and self-perceived mental health. Researchers also measured participants'overall
satisfaction around cooking and diet-related behaviors.
What were the findings? Course participants saw significant improvements in general health. They also reported
improved mental health and subjective vitality immediately after the program. [19] These benefits remained six months
after the completion of the course.
What caused these improvements? Researchers have previously found a link between eating more fruits and vegetables, and improved longer term mental health. This would imply that the participants in the current study may have felt better due to improved diet.
However, the study showed participants'mental health improved even if their reported diet did not change after
completing the program. Also, the mental health benefits were equal among participants who were overweight or obese,
and those in a healthy weight range. [20] This suggests a link between cooking confidence and satisfaction around
cooking, and mental health benefits.
[21] Who benefits most from learning to cook? Gender plays a part. At the start of the program, 77 per cent of
female participants were confident about cooking, but just 23 per cent of males were confident. At the end of the
program, cooking confidence and skills were equal across both counterparts. This change in confidence could lead to a
gender balance in home cooking.This in turn could reduce consumption of unhealthy,high-calorie processed meals.

[22] What is personal space? We often think of it as an invisible bubble of space surrounding us that others can't
enter, without causing discomfort. Research shows, however, that we actually have bubbles of different sizes. Each of
these bubbles applies to a different set of people.
The smallest zone, called "intimate space", extends outward from our bodies 18 inches in every direction
Only family, pets and one's closest friends may enter it. [23]A mere acquaintance entering our intimate space makes
us uncomfortable. Next is the bubble called personal space", extending from 1.5 feet to 4 feet away. Friends and
acquaintances can comfortably occupy this zone, especially during informal conversations, but strangers are forbidden.
[24] Extending from 4 to 12 feet away from us is “"social space". Here people feel comfortable conducting routine
social interactions with new acquaintances or total strangers.
Those are the average sizes of American's personal bubbles, anyway. It is important to keep in mind that personal
space varies depending on culture and context. Furthermore, there are significant individual differences. As we all
know, cultural or individual differences in personal bubble diameters are all too often the cause of discomfort. How did
these personal bubbles arise? According to research, we begin to develop our individual sense of personal space around
age 3 or 4. [25] The sizes of our bubbles are fixed by our teens. These bubbles are constructed and monitored by the
brain region involved in fear.
